extracted.intended_audience: Supreme Court justices, appellate lawyers, patent practitioners, medical professionals and clinical laboratories affected by gene patents
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluation of whether isolated human genes (BRCA1 and BRCA2) and related claims are patent-eligible subject matter under U.S. patent law, as presented to the Supreme Court in Association for Molecular Pathology v. Myriad Genetics. The petition frames related issues about method-claim eligibility under Mayo and standing under MedImmune but is limited to the gene-patentability question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Are human genes patentable?
rubrics_metrics.description: Many patients seek genetic testing for mutations associated with increased cancer risk. Respondent Myriad Genetics obtained patents on two human genes (BRCA1 and BRCA2) claiming every naturally-occurring version of those genes, including mutations, on the theory that Myriad invented something patent-eligible simply by removing ("isolating") the genes from the body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion asks whether claims to isolated human genes constitute patentable subject matter (e.g., "composition of matter") or are precluded as naturally occurring products. Considerations include whether isolation transforms the naturally occurring DNA into a patent-eligible invention, whether claiming all naturally-occurring variants (including mutations) is permissible, and the practical effect on diagnostic testing and medical practice. Note: the petition as filed was limited to Question 1 (the gene-patentability issue) and certiorari was granted on that question.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the court of appeals erred in upholding a method claim inconsistent with Mayo v. Prometheus
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners assert that the court of appeals upheld a Myriad method claim that is irreconcilable with this Court's ruling in Mayo Collaborative Servs. v. Prometheus Labs., Inc., 132 S. Ct. 1289 (2012).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion evaluates method-claim eligibility in light of the Mayo decision, which addresses patent claims that effectively cover natural laws, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas when implemented using well-understood, routine, conventional activity. Apply Mayo's framework: determine whether the claim is directed to a natural law or phenomenon and, if so, whether it recites an inventive concept sufficient to transform the nature of the claim into patent-eligible subject matter. Assess compatibility of the appealed method claim with Mayo's standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Whether the court of appeals adopted an incorrect standing rule contrary to MedImmune
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioners contend the court of appeals adopted a new and inflexible rule, contrary to normal standing rules and MedImmune, Inc. v. Genentech, Inc., 549 U.S. 118 (2007), that petitioners who have been indisputably deterred by Myriad's "active enforcement" nonetheless lack standing to challenge those patents absent evidence they have been personally threatened with an infringement action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion examines whether the appeals court's standing analysis improperly requires an explicit threat or actual lawsuit before affected parties (e.g., medical professionals using routine genetic testing) may seek declaratory judgment or otherwise challenge patent validity. Consider MedImmune's allowance for pre-enforcement challenges where a reasonable apprehension of suit exists and assess whether deterrence from active enforcement suffices to establish standing under constitutional and prudential doctrines.
